abstract: This Brookings Metro analysis examines the geographic distribution of generative AI's workforce impacts across U.S. counties and metropolitan areas. Unlike previous automation technologies that disrupted lower-skilled, rural workers, generative AI exposure is concentrated in high-skill, high-wage urban metros due to its facility with cognitive office work. The study finds that workers in tech hubs like San Jose face much greater AI exposure (43% could see half or more of tasks affected) compared to less information-oriented metros like Las Vegas (31%), reversing historical automation patterns that favored educated urban areas.
keyFindings: More than 30% of all U.S. workers could see at least 50% of their occupational tasks affected by generative AI, with 85% potentially experiencing at least 10% task impact.
43% of workers in San Jose could experience generative AI shifting half or more of their tasks, compared to only 31% in Las Vegas, reflecting urban-rural divergence.

High-skill metropolitan areas such as San Jose, San Francisco, Durham, New York, and Washington D.C. face the heaviest generative AI exposure, while less office-oriented metros like Las Vegas, Toledo, and Fort Wayne show far lower susceptibility.

County-level AI exposure ranges from 40% or more in tech-focused areas (Santa Clara County at 42.8%) to as low as 20% in rural heartland counties, with average metro exposure at 35% versus 30% in rural counties.

Generative AI's geographic impact pattern inverts previous automation trends: rather than disrupting lower-skill rural workers, it most affects higher-educated white-collar workers in information-oriented cities.
methodology: Analysis based on occupation-specific AI exposure ratings from OpenAI (Eloundou et al., 2023) covering 858 occupations, of which 738 unique Standard Occupational Classification codes matched Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS) data. The authors calculated average exposure ratings for grouped SOC codes and multiplied these by local occupational employment figures, aggregating results to compute county- and metropolitan-level exposure statistics. Geographic analysis leveraged OEWS employment data to determine the share of AI-exposed jobs relative to total local employment in each U.S. county and metropolitan area.
qualifiers: 'Exposure' does not speak only to worker displacement; it may also involve worker 'augmentation' through improved AI tools that enhance productivity and capability. The analysis reflects possible patterns and forecasts rather than definitive predictions. Previous automation analysis patterns cited are from Brookings' earlier research; the current study builds on but does not replicate those findings. The exposure ratings are from OpenAI data 'supplied over a year ago' relative to the February 2025 publication date.
